newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia's Taylor signs bill on peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: Liberia's Taylor signs bill on peacekeepers.

text.p: Liberia's President Charles Taylor said he had signed his first bill after parliament passed an act seeking to define the role of peacekeepers.

A new parliament began sitting on Monday for the first time since civil war erupted in Liberia in 1989. On Tuesday it passed its first act dealing with the force stationed in Liberia by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) since 1990.
"I have signed a bill requiring this government to enter a status of forces agreement within 30 days as of today," Taylor said in a speech at a banquet for lawmakers on Tuesday night.
The 26-member Senate and the 64-seat lower house passed the bill at a joint session which also enacted a second law reaffirming the supremacy of Liberia's 1986 constitution.
The law on peacekeepers seeks to restrict the role of the Nigerian-led force from 10 nations to purely security, leaving civil and criminal matters to police and the judiciary.
The law also empowers Taylor to seek agreement with ECOWAS on cuts in the peacekeepig force known as ECOMOG, now numbering about 10,500 troops.
It was first passed in early 1996 by an unelected interim assembly with limited legislative powers. ECOWAS said only an elected Liberian president could sign the forces agreement.
No vote was required for the bill's passage on Tuesday.

Taylor launched Liberia's civil war with an invasion by his guerrillas from neighbouring Ivory Coast in December 1989. He came close to taking the capital Monrovia in 1990 and 1992 but was blocked by ECOMOG on each occasion.
Frustrated, Taylor demanded an agreement to curtail the powers of the peacekeeping force.
But Taylor changed tack earlier this year as he prepared to run for president after ECOMOG was given a stronger mandate to disarm guerrillas and provide security for the polls.

Taylor, who took office last Saturday, said in February that he wanted ECOMOG to stay 12 or 18 months longer. But he would prefer a redefined mandate placing the force under the aurthority of the Liberian president.
ECOWAS is expected to take a decision on the future of the force when the bloc holds its full summit later this month or early September.
The second act passed by lawmakers endorsed the 1986 constitution as "the supreme and fundamental law of Liberia and provisions shall continue to have binding force and effect".
Liberia was founded by freed American slaves in 1847, and its constitution until 1986 was based on that of the United States.
Meanwhile Taylor faced criticism for the first time as president, with many Liberians denouncing his new cabinet as dominated by his National Patriotic Party loyalists or defectors from other camps.

"Not that those being appointed are not qualified, but that the appointment does not have any semblance of a government of inclusion," an editorial in the independent Inquirer newspaper said in a typical comment.
The 18 people appointed to Taylor's cabinet include three former rivals, notably ethnic-Krahn champion General Roosevelt Johnson. Two senior cabinet posts are vacant.
No job has yet been offered to any of his losing presidential rivals as urged by foreign donors as a guarantee of peace.
